"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 1: The connection as a state machine.

A server is not a `for` loop over reads. It is a policy about who gets the
processor next, and the thing it holds is a *connection*: something that is not
yet readable, then readable, then owed a reply, then not writable yet, then
done — five phases, and every one of them a fact about the wire rather than a
line of the loop. This stage builds the smallest honest version of that: one
connection, carried as data in a dict, moved one step at a time by the caller.
It is the ladder's root because the four models above it (blocking, thread,
reactor, event loop) disagree about nothing except *who* calls `step_conn` and
in what order.

The world is `link.py`, and it is provided: a `Client` scripted with the requests
it sends, a `Connection` the server accepts and answers, bytes carried one
`MAX_CHUNK` at a time, and a bounded outbox whose short write is backpressure
rather than an error. Nothing here calls the server; the server calls the link,
and the link keeps the log every later stage is graded against. The link is also
the only clock: `Link.step()` is the one thing that moves a byte, which is why a
stage that cannot move anything must say so with an event instead of spinning.

Two facts about the protocol decide most of the code below. A request is *one
line ending in `\\n`*, and a reply is that line with `REPLY_PREFIX` in front of
it — so the machine may not answer until it has a whole line, and it may not
assume a line arrives in one read, because `MAX_CHUNK` is how much one move
carries and not how long a request may be. And a client sends its next request
only once it has drained the answer to the one before, so a machine that is
waiting for the drain and a machine whose client is done look alike on the wire;
telling those two apart is this stage's real decision.

    STATES       the five phases, in the order a well-behaved connection meets
                 them: new → reading → writing → reading → … → closing → closed
    REPLY_PREFIX the one byte of protocol stages 1–8 speak
    open_conn    the machine for a connection, in `"new"`
    step_conn    one move: read, write, or the honest `"idle"`
    finish       `closing → closed`: hand the connection back to the link
    stats        requests, replies, bytes_read, bytes_written — from the machine

`ServerError` is the family, and every refusal names the offender: the id the
link never made, the limit that is not 1 to `MAX_CHUNK`, the phase no machine
has, the connection that is another link's, the `finish` from a phase that is not
`"closing"`. A verdict about what the *client* did is never an exception: a spent
patience, a partial line and a full outbox are phases and events.

DESIGN DECISION — what does the connection's state carry, and who owns it?
Every function hands back a *fresh* dict: `"state"` (the phase), `"conn"` (the
link's own connection object), `"buffer"` (the line assembled so far), `"out"`
(the reply the outbox has not taken yet) and the four counters `stats` reports.
A step returns that dict plus `"event"`, `"reply"` and `"bytes"`, so `state =
step_conn(link, state)` is the whole of driving a connection and `stats(state)`
answers about the machine and not about a copy of it. Nothing is kept at module
level and nothing is written into the caller's dict.

DESIGN DECISION — why is `"idle"` an event rather than an error, and why is a
zero-byte read not one either?
Because "nothing to read now" is the commonest thing that happens to a server:
the client is still typing, the outbox is full, the reply is in flight and the
next request arrives only after the drain. `link.read` answers `b""` for exactly
that, and a machine that treats `b""` as a failure is a machine that cannot wait
— which is every server there is. `"idle"` also makes the step count honest: a
model that steps when nothing can move is a busy-wait, and this event is how the
count says so.

DESIGN DECISION — when is the reply staged, and why is the reply line rebuilt
per line?
Only when the buffer ends in `\\n`: a request is one line, so a reply written
before the whole line was read is an answer to half a question — the framing bug
every stream protocol has. The buffer is *rebuilt* (emptied) the moment its line
is answered, because the reply the client is owed is the line that was just read
and not the conversation so far; a buffer that is kept across requests turns the
second answer into the first one repeated. `REPLY_PREFIX` is applied once, at
the moment the line becomes a reply, and never again while the outbox takes it
in pieces.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the machine never close a connection itself, and how
does it know the client has no more requests?
`finish` is the only thing that closes, and only from `"closing"`: reaching
`"closing"` is how the read side says the client has nothing left to send and
has taken every byte it was written, and a connection closed before that is a
reply dropped after the server had already answered. Since a client that is
about to send its next request looks idle on the wire, the machine asks the world
the only question with an answer — is there a further request in this client's
script? — and the link being the one that scripts the client is exactly why that
is honest rather than a guess.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a step take a `limit`, and why does the reply not
have to fit the outbox?
`limit` is a *move* budget, `MAX_CHUNK` at most, because the link carries bytes
in pieces and a server that read a request in one call would be a server that
assumed the line arrived whole. A reply longer than the outbox is the same fact
one direction over: the world takes what it can and hands back a count, and a
server that ignores that count reports bytes it never delivered. So the tail
stays in `"out"` and the machine stays in `"writing"` — the deferred write is

#: The five phases of one connection, in the order a well-behaved one meets
#: them. `new → reading → writing → reading → …` for the client's requests, then
#: `closing → closed` once `finish` has handed the connection back to the link.
STATES = ("new", "reading", "writing", "closing", "closed")

#: The one byte of protocol stages 1–8 speak: the reply is the request line with
#: this in front of it. It is a `str` because it is a protocol character, and it
#: is a single byte so that the reply is one byte longer than the line and never
#: two; a check that sees the prefix twice sees a server that rebuilt a reply it
#: had already built.
REPLY_PREFIX = "+"


class ServerError(ValueError):
    """A connection this stage will not open, step or close, named as what is wrong.

    It is the family for every shape the machine cannot honour: a connection id
    the link never made, a limit that is not 1 to `MAX_CHUNK`, a phase no state
    machine has, a connection that belongs to another link, and a `finish` from a
    phase that is not `"closing"`. A verdict about what the *client* did is never
    an exception here: a spent patience, a partial line and a full outbox are all
    phases or events, and a check asserts them as values.
    """


def open_conn(link, cid):
    """The machine for connection `cid`, in the `"new"` phase.

    `link.connection(cid)` is the validation and the whole of it: a `cid` that is
    not an int, or is not a connection this link made, is refused naming what was
    given. The `"state"` handed back is the machine's own dict — a fresh one
    every time, so that nothing the caller keeps is ever the stage's to write.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement open_conn()")


def step_conn(link, state, *, limit=MAX_CHUNK):
    """One move of one connection: read the request, or write the reply.

    The answer is `{"state", "event", "reply", "bytes"}` *and* the machine's own
    fields, because this is the whole of driving a connection: `state =
    step_conn(link, state)`, and `stats(state)` when the run is over. One move
    per call and never two — `"read"` takes up to `limit` bytes of the request
    into the buffer, `"write"` hands what the outbox will take of the staged
    reply to the link, `"accepted"` is the `new → reading` step, and `"idle"` is
    the honest answer when there is nothing to read or nowhere to write: closing
    a connection, or reading `b""` as a failure, is the mistake this event exists
    to make impossible.

    A request is one line, so a reply is staged only once the buffer ends in
    `"\\n"` — `limit` is how much one *move* carries (`MAX_CHUNK` at most), never
    how long a request may be, and a line that arrives in three moves is read in
    three. The reply the outbox cannot take stays in the state as `"out"`, and
    the machine stays in `"writing"` until the link has carried it; a connection
    the link has closed (the client's patience spent) leaves the machine in
    `"closing"` rather than forever hoping to write.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement step_conn()")


def finish(link, state):
    """`closing → closed`: the connection is handed back to the link, once.

    This is the one transition the machine does not make while stepping, and it
    is deliberately not a step: a connection is closed from `"closing"` and from
    nowhere else, because reaching `"closing"` is exactly the read side saying
    that the client has no request left and has taken every answer. Closing is
    idempotent — a machine already `"closed"` answers `"idle"` and changes
    nothing — and any other phase is refused, naming it.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement finish()")


def stats(state):
    """What this machine has done: `{"requests", "replies", "bytes_read",
    "bytes_written"}`.

    A request is counted when its line is whole and its reply staged, a reply
    when the last of its bytes has been written — so a client that dropped
    before its answer moved leaves the two numbers different, which is the
    point. `bytes_read` and `bytes_written` are what the link's own calls moved,
    so a check can hold them against `link.stats()` and notice a machine that
    believed it wrote what the outbox never took.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement stats()")

"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 2: The blocking server, and the slow client.

Stage 1 built the connection as data and one move at a time, and it deliberately
did not say who calls those moves or in what order. This stage answers the first
half of that question the only way a single-threaded server can: one client at a
time, each one driven to completion before the next is even accepted. Accept, read
the line, answer, wait for the client to drain the answer, close the connection,
take the next client — and only then look at anybody else. It is the model
Bendersky's series starts from, and it is worth writing by hand precisely because
it is defensible: it is simple, it is correct for a handful of clients, and it
contains the failure the whole course is about.

The bundle is `{"link", "clients", "requests"}`: the world, the scripted clients
it holds, and the lines those clients send. This stage adds nothing to that
bundle and reads nothing else out of it — the link is the arbiter of what is
really on the wire, and the policies above this stage (threads, a reactor, timers,
callbacks, `async`) are handed exactly the same dict. What they disagree about is
who gets the processor next; this stage's answer is "whoever was accepted first,
and nobody else until they are finished".

The failure is the slow client. A client that drains its inbox every fourth tick
is a perfectly ordinary client; under a blocking server it is a stop-the-world
event, because the one thread of control has nothing to do but turn the world's
clock until that client has taken its bytes. Everyone behind it waits, and the
budget — counted in *steps*, one turn of the loop each — is what makes that
visible: the model returns what it managed instead of pretending it finished.

    serve_blocking  the whole model: accept, read, answer, wait, close; repeat

The result is the model's verdict about the run, and it is the same shape every
later model has to produce, so the capstone can compare four of them:

    answers   {name: tuple of the reply lines the server wrote, in order} — every
              client of the bundle is present; a client the budget never reached
              is an empty tuple rather than a missing key
    steps     the turns the loop took (one turn = one move plus one tick)
    ticks     the link's clock at the end of the run
    served    the clients taken to completion, in that order
    starved   the clients whose requests the server never answered, in accept
              order — not "everyone who is not served"

DESIGN DECISION — what is a turn, and why does every turn tick the world?
A turn is one move of the current connection's stage-1 machine, and the turn ends
by handing the link one tick. A blocking server has one thread of control: while
it reads, while it writes and while it waits for the client to drain, it cannot do
anything else, and in this course the link only moves a byte or a clock when it
is stepped. So the two counts come out equal — `steps == ticks` — and that
equality is the finding rather than an accident of implementation: every
operation this model performs costs every client a tick of the world's time. A
model that let some turns pass without ticking would be reporting a cost it did
not pay.

DESIGN DECISION — in what order are the clients served, and does the model ever
prefer one?
In the order the link offers them: `accept()` is the oldest waiting client, and
the loop takes the next one only after `finish` has closed the current one. The
model has no policy to choose, and that is the point — a blocking server's only
scheduling decision is "the one in front", which is why one slow client stops
everyone. `served` therefore comes out in accept order, and a model whose
`served` does not is a model that reordered its clients, not a model that blocked.

DESIGN DECISION — what is `answers`, and who counts a reply as written?
A reply is written when the last of its bytes has gone into the link's outbox,
which is stage 1's own count (`"replies"`): a reply the bounded outbox only half
took is *not* an answer yet, and the pieces it went out in are not two answers.
The entries are therefore whole lines, prefix and newline included, and the reply
is attributed to the connection the model is serving and to no other. Every
client of the bundle appears, with an empty tuple when the run never answered it,
because a dict with missing keys cannot be compared across models and a client
the budget cut off is a fact worth reporting.

DESIGN DECISION — exactly which clients are `starved`?
The clients with at least one request the server never answered, in accept order.
The tempting shortcut — everyone who is not in `served` — is wrong on both sides.
A client sitting in the backlog has a request the link holds and no answer, so it
is starved; a client whose request was read and answered, but whose connection
the budget stopped the model from draining and closing, is neither served nor
starved, and calling it starved would hide the very thing the budget is there to
show. The verdict is derived from the link's own count of each client's requests
and the answers the model actually wrote.

DESIGN DECISION — what happens when the budget runs out, and why is that not an
exception?
A budget is a count of steps, and the loop takes a turn only while it has one
left: check, then move, so a budget of N is exactly N turns and never N+1. When
the budget is spent the model stops and returns what it did — `served`, `starved`
and the answers written so far — because "I did not finish" is a legitimate
answer to "serve these clients within this many steps", and the caller can hold it
against the link's log. Only a shape the model cannot honour at all is a
refusal: a bundle that is not `{"link", "clients", "requests"}` with a link whose
own connections agree with it, or a budget that is not a count of steps.

"""


class ServerError(ValueError):
    """A server bundle this stage will not serve, or a budget that is not a count.

    It is the family for every shape `serve_blocking` cannot honour: a `server`
    that is not a dict, one that is missing one of its three keys, a `"link"`

    with the link's own connections, a `"requests"` mapping without one of those

    exception here: a client the budget never reached is `starved`, and a budget
    spent with work left is an outcome the caller reads out of the result.
    """


def serve_blocking(server, *, budget=256):
    """Serve the bundle's clients one at a time, to completion, inside a budget.

    The loop is the oldest server there is: take the oldest waiting client, drive
    its stage-1 machine until the client has nothing left to send and has taken
    every byte the server wrote, close it, and only then look at the next one.
    No second client's request is ever read while the first is unanswered, which
    is what makes the model *blocking* — and what makes a client that drains its
    inbox every fourth tick the whole story of the run.

    One turn is one move of the current connection, and every turn lets the link
    move one tick, because the model has nothing to do but wait while the world
    carries the bytes and the client drains them. `steps` counts turns and
    `ticks` is the link's clock at the end; on this model they are equal, and
    that equality is the cost of a single thread of control.

    `answers` carries every client of the bundle, in the link's accept order: the
    reply lines the server wrote for it, in order, as whole lines (a reply the
    outbox took in two pieces is one entry), and an empty tuple for a client the
    budget never reached. `served` is the order the clients were taken to
    completion — for a blocking model the accept order — and `starved` is the
    clients with a request the server never answered, again in accept order.

    `budget` is a count of *steps*: the loop takes a turn only while it has one
    left, so a budget spent with work left is a result rather than an exception,
    and the caller can tell from `served`, `starved` and the link's own
    `bytes_drained` exactly how far it got.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement serve_blocking()")

"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 3: Threads, and the interleaving the check chooses.

Stage 2 served one client at a time, to completion, and the slow client stopped
everyone behind it. The repair is not a thread library: it is *concurrency as a
choice* — N connections, each carried by something that does one small step and
gives the processor back, and an order that is data somebody handed in rather
than luck. That "something" is a *step function*: called once per turn, it owns
no stack, keeps whatever it needs between turns in the arguments it was spawned
with, and answers exactly one of `"more"`, `"blocked"` or `"done"`. This stage is
the machinery behind that word — `Scheduler` — and the policy that uses it, one
thread per connection over stage 1's state machine.

Why the interleaving is data: a real thread library hands the order to the
operating system, so the run that failed is not reproducible and the run that
passed is not evidence. Here the *script* is a tuple of thread names, the check
chooses it, and the result says what the choice cost — `steps` is the number of
turns taken and `order` is the order the answers went out. A blocked thread is a
verdict rather than an exception: a thread waiting for something another thread
must do is fine, and a round in which *every* remaining thread is waiting is a
deadlock, reported with the names.

`threading`, `asyncio` and `time` are banned in this course for exactly this
reason: the interleaving is the subject, the clock is the link's, and the model
is a loop the caller can drive. What a step function must *not* do: spin on a
read that will never return anything, close a connection it has not finished
answering, or keep its state in a module-level variable where the next run can
find it.

    STEP_STATES  the three answers a step function may give
    THREAD_STATES what the scheduler calls a thread between turns
    Scheduler    spawn, ready, step, run: N step functions and whose turn it is
    serve_threads  one thread per connection, with the script as the interleaving

`ServerError` is the family, and every refusal names the offender: the name that
is not a name, the step function that is not callable, the name already spawned,
the script entry nobody spawned, the turn for a thread that has finished, the
answer that is not one of `STEP_STATES`, the budget that is not a count, and the
`server` whose three pieces do not describe one workload. A verdict about what
the *threads* did — blocked, deadlocked, starved — is always returned, never
raised.

DESIGN DECISION — what does a thread keep, given that it has no stack?
The alternative is a closure or a module-level table, and both are worse in the
same way: a closure hides the state where a check cannot see it, and a module
table means two runs of the same workload are not two runs. So `spawn(name, fn,
*args)` calls `fn(*args)` and the state a thread carries between turns lives in
those arguments — for `serve_threads`, one context per connection holding stage
1's machine, the reply it is halfway through writing, and the lists it reports
into. A step function is then a plain function of its own memory, which is
exactly what makes it testable one turn at a time.

DESIGN DECISION — is `"blocked"` a death sentence or a round verdict?
It is a round verdict, and the difference is the whole point: a thread blocked
waiting for another thread's turn has to get that turn back once the others have
had theirs, or nothing would ever unblock it. So a blocked thread is skipped by
the round-robin, a scripted turn for one is spent without calling anything, and
the block is cleared when every remaining thread has been offered a turn — *unless*
the whole round blocked, which is a deadlock and is returned as
`{"finished": False, "blocked": (names…)}` rather than cleared away.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the scheduler know nothing about the link?
Because the two questions are separable, and keeping them apart is what makes
this stage reusable: `Scheduler` counts turns and holds state, and the world
moves only when a thread spends a turn on `Link.step()`. The alternative — a
scheduler that ticks the clock itself — would make `serve_threads` the only
model it can ever drive, and stage 7's loop, which is this same loop desugared,
would need its own copy.

DESIGN DECISION — who spends a turn when a connection's thread has nothing to move?
`serve_threads` spends it on the world's tick. A client drains its inbox on its
own schedule and the link carries an outbox only when the clock moves, so a
thread that had nothing to move and simply answered `"blocked"` would be waiting
for a turn that nobody has any reason to take. The tick is therefore the model's
wait — and because it is counted, a model that waits too much cannot hide it.

DESIGN DECISION — why report `"state"` and `"yielded"` when one is derived from the other?
Because the two vocabularies answer different questions: `"yielded"` is what the
step function said (`"more"`, `"blocked"`, `"done"`) and `"state"` is where the
scheduler records the thread (`"ready"`, `"blocked"`, `"done"`). A caller that
only has the second cannot tell a turn that was taken from a turn that was
skipped — a skipped turn yields `None` — and a check that cannot tell those apart
cannot see a thread counted as a step when it never ran.

not a name, a callback that is not callable, a handle this table never issued, a

verdict about what the *world* did is never an exception — a connection whose
client gave up, a callback the loop cancelled, and a callback whose connection
had closed are all results, and the check asserts them as values.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a callback a 4-tuple in a table instead of a closure
over the loop?
A closure is what everybody writes first, and it is what makes the loop's own
variables part of the callback's behaviour: `handles.append(lambda: answer(conn,
line))` captures `conn` and `line` *by reference*, so by the time the callback
runs, both may belong to the next connection of the turn. The bug is invisible
until two connections are served in one turn, and then it is silent: the last
client's line is answered twice and the first client's answer never comes. The
4-tuple makes the per-connection state `args` — data the callback carries, which
nothing the loop does afterwards can change. Everything else in this stage
follows from that one choice: the table can be inspected, cancelled, and asked
for its order, because a callback is a value and not a stack frame.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a callback whose connection has closed a `skipped`
verdict rather than an exception?
Because it is the *common* case, not the exceptional one: a client that waited
too long for an answer it can no longer be given has done nothing wrong, and a
server that raises for it is a server that has to wrap every dispatch in a
`try`. Worse, an exception here would have to be caught somewhere, and the
natural place to catch it — around the loop — ends the whole run because one
client hung up. So the verdict is returned: the callback is taken out of the
table, its name goes into `skipped`, and the loop goes on. The name matters as
much as the count, because "a callback was skipped" is not a fact anybody can
act on and "gamma's callback for its first request was skipped" is.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `ready()` leave cancelled handles out, and why is
`take` a separate move from `ready`?
A table that keeps a cancelled callback "for the record" is a table that runs it
later: the caller cancelled it and then the loop, reading its own order list,
found it again. So cancelling removes it from the count of what can run, and
`ready` is the only thing the loop is allowed to look at when it decides what is
next. Splitting `ready` from `take` is the same decision one step further: `ready`
is a question ("what is there") and `take` is a move ("give me that one and drop
it"), so a loop that dispatches pops exactly one callback rather than iterating a
list it is mutating — the classic bug of skipping every second element. Asking
for a handle there is nothing for is a verdict, `None`; asking with something
that is not a handle at all is a shape, and that is refused.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the loop dispatch one callback per turn, and what is
the budget a budget of?
If a turn drained the whole table, the callback that runs last would run in the
same tick as the one that runs first, and the queue would be a fiction: nothing
could ever happen in between, so nothing could ever cancel a callback, close a
connection under one, or have a run that stops with callbacks still queued. One
dispatch per turn makes the queue the thing the stage is about, and makes `steps`
a count of callbacks dispatched. `budget` then bounds turns, which is a bound on
work and not on time — and a budget spent with callbacks still in the table is an
outcome, not an exception. The loop says what it did with them: the callbacks it
never reached are cancelled by name when their connection is fine, and skipped
when it has closed, so nothing is quietly kept and run on some later turn that
never comes.

DESIGN DECISION — when is a connection finished, and why is that not "when its
reply was written"?
Because writing a reply is not delivering it. `Link.write` puts bytes in the
outbox and `Link.step` carries them into the client's inbox, where they sit until
the client's own drain schedule takes them — a client that reads every fourth
tick holds its answer for four ticks. A loop that closes the connection as soon
as the write returned cuts that client off mid-answer, and the server's own
report would not show it: the link's `bytes_drained` is the number that does. So
finished means three things at once — the client has no more requests to send,
the link has nothing to read, owe or carry, and the client has drained everything
it was sent — and the loop is over when its own connections are all closed *and*
the listener is holding nobody, because a client that arrives on a later tick is
still a client to serve.

`serve_callbacks`.

    callable, a handle this table never issued, a server that is not a server,
    and a budget that is not a positive count of turns. A verdict about what the
    *world* did is never an exception: a connection whose client's patience ran
    out, a callback the loop cancelled and a callback whose connection had
    closed are all results, and the check asserts them as values.
    """

    The table owns three facts and no others. `_order` is every handle this
    table has issued, in registration order, which is what makes `ready` an
    order and not a set. `_table` is the callbacks still to run, keyed by
    handle: `take` and `cancel` both remove from it, so a handle leaves the
    table exactly once. `_gone` is the handles that have left it, which is why
    cancelling twice is not an error and why a handle that was never issued is.

    Nothing here is a closure and nothing here is a loop variable: a callback
    is the 4-tuple `(handle, name, fn, args)`, and `args` is the whole of what
    the callback will know when it runs.
    """

        raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement Handles.__init__()")

    def register(self, name, fn, *args):

        registration order of a table is the order of its handles. `name` is
        what the result will call this callback when it ran, was skipped or was
        cancelled, so it has to be a non-empty string; `fn` is what will be
        called with `args` when its turn comes, so it has to be callable.

        late-binding bug gets wrong.

        raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement Handles.register()")

        is the caller's move and the table has no opinion about why. A handle
        this table never issued is a refusal naming it — a cancellation that
        silently did nothing is a callback that runs after the code that tried to
        stop it. Cancelling a handle that is already gone answers `False`: the
        first cancel is the one that changed the table.
        """

        it "for the record" would be a table that runs it. The order is the
        registration order and never the order of cancelling or taking, because
        the order of callbacks is the order a server promised its clients.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 6: implement Handles.ready()")

        not there is how a loop says "nothing for me this time" — while a handle

    callback's own name, from its own `args`, and never the loop's last
    connection. `steps` is the turns the loop took, one per dispatch, so a
    `budget` spent with callbacks still queued is an outcome and not an
    exception. `ran` is the names of the callbacks that ran, in the order they
    ran, and that order is the registration order.

"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 7: Futures and async/await as a desugaring.

`async` and `await` are not a runtime, they are a *desugaring*. A coroutine is a
step function that answers `{"wait": True}` while it cannot go on and
`{"value": …}` when it can; `await` is a function that decides which of the two a
future has earned; and the loop that calls those step functions is the very event
loop stages 4 to 6 already built. This stage writes that desugaring out in full,
with **no `async def` anywhere** and `asyncio` banned outright, because the thing
worth knowing is that a promise, a yield and a driver are three pieces of *data*
— and that the loop was never the magic part.

The three pieces, in the order they meet. A `Future` is one answer, settled once:
a second `settle` is a refusal, `value()` before it is settled is a refusal, and
`result()` is how a caller asks *without* an exception — `{"done", "value"}`, the
question a `then` callback asks. `await_` is the whole of the `await` keyword:
handed a settled future it answers `{"value": …}`, handed one that is not it
answers `{"wait": True}`, and that dict is exactly a step function's answer, so a
coroutine written by hand is `lambda: await_(future)` and nothing else. `chain` is
the smallest driver there is — one coroutine, stepped to its answer — and `Loop`
is the real one: many coroutines, an order the *check* chooses, and a budget in
steps.

Then the server, which is the point of the whole course: `serve_async` accepts
every client the link is holding, gives each connection a coroutine that drives
stage 1's state machine, and lets the loop drive them. Nothing here is a thread
and nothing here sleeps: `Link.step()` is the only thing that moves a byte, so
the driver steps the world between turns, and every number in the result — the
steps, the ticks, the four orders — is recomputable from what the link logged.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a coroutine a step function answering a dict, instead of
an `async def` and a real `await`?
    Because the loop is the subject and `async def` hides it. A coroutine that is
    a step function can be called by anybody, in any order, any number of times —
    which is exactly what a check needs in order to *choose* the interleaving —
    and "am I ready" stops being a language feature and becomes a dict this stage
    can assert on. `asyncio` is banned here for the same reason `threading` was
    banned in stage 3: a course that cannot step its own concurrency cannot
    report a step count, and the step count is the only honest score there is.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a future settled exactly once, and what does `result()`
buy that `value()` does not?
    A promise that can change its answer is not a promise: a coroutine that
    resumed on the first settlement could be resumed again on the second, and the
    bug reads as "the callback ran twice" long after the second `settle` went in.
    Settling once, and *refusing* the second with the value the future already
    holds in the message, makes that impossible rather than unlikely. And the two
    reads are two different questions: `value()` is for the caller that has
    already asked `done()` and wants to be told when it was wrong, while
    `result()` is for the caller that must not raise — `{"done": False, "value":
    None}` is an answer about an unsettled future, and every callback written
    against a promise needs that answer.

DESIGN DECISION — what is `chain` for, when `Loop` already drives coroutines, and
why does it have a bound?
    `chain` is the one-coroutine case, and it is where the desugaring is easiest
    to see: a coroutine that answers `{"wait": True}` forever is a coroutine
    waiting on a future nobody settled, and a coroutine that answers on its first
    call is an `await` on a settled one. The bound is because `chain` has no world
    to drive: it cannot settle anything, so a coroutine that never answers would

    budget; the chain's job is to say where one coroutine got to.

"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 8: Backpressure, and the write that has to be deferred.

Stage 1 gave a connection a bounded outbox and said the truth about it: `write`
hands back how many bytes the outbox took, and a short write is *data*, not an
error. Stage 4's reactor then serviced every ready connection once a turn, and
every reply went out in one move because every reply in that stage's workload was
smaller than the outbox. This stage takes the promise seriously: a reply that is
bigger than `MAX_CHUNK`, and a reply bigger than the outbox, are written over
several turns, and the connection's state — not a local variable, not a closure —
carries what is left.

`send` is one move of one connection's reply: it hands over the bytes still owed,
counts what the world took, and answers with `sent`, `deferred` and `drained`.
`serve_backpressure` is a reactor-shaped loop around it — the ready set is
stage 4's, the poll is once a turn, the link is stepped once a turn — whose write
side is deliberately one reply at a time. That is the decision this stage exists
for: with a single write path, one reply that cannot be finished blocks every
reply behind it, and the number of turns a client's answer spends waiting for a
turn it never gets is exactly what `stalled` reports.

TODO: implement `send` and `serve_backpressure` in stage_08.py.

DESIGN DECISION — where does the part of the reply the outbox could not take go?

The world's `write` returns a count, and the caller owns the rest. It must not
live in a local variable of the loop — a loop that keeps a reply "in flight" in a
local is a loop that loses it the moment another connection is serviced — and it
must not be grown into the outbox, which is the world's bound and not the
server's to widen. So the connection's state carries the reply being written and
how far it has got: `pending` (the reply in flight, whole, while it is unfinished)
and `offset` (how many of its bytes have reached the outbox). The bytes still owed
are `pending[offset:]`, `deferred` is their count, and a state whose `pending` is
empty is a connection with nothing owed — the same state a reply starts from.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a second `send` of the same reply a refusal?

A reply that takes several turns is a reply whose caller has to remember the
offset across turns. A caller that hands over the same bytes again — the whole
reply, after part of it has already reached the outbox — is a caller that has lost
the offset, and a server that repeats a reply's opening bytes is a server whose
client sees a corrupted answer. So a `send` on a connection whose `pending` is
non-empty must hand over exactly the bytes still owed: `pending[offset:]`, the
tail the state itself implies. Anything else is refused, naming what was given,
because a refusal here is cheap and a doubled reply is not.

DESIGN DECISION — does a server that defers writes service every connection each turn?

It cannot, and pretending otherwise is what hides the subject. The write side of
this loop is one reply at a time, in the order the replies were staged: the
connection at the head of that queue gets one outbox-full per turn until its
client has taken the whole answer, and only then does the next reply start. Serve
every pending connection a byte each turn and head-of-line blocking disappears —
and with it the honest number a student should see, because the client behind the
slow one is waiting for a turn the server has not got. `stalled` names the
connections the whole budget left with a reply that never moved: that is the same
fact as "one slow reader costs everyone behind it", expressed as a count instead
of an apology.

DESIGN DECISION — what does `send` do when the world takes nothing?

It answers, rather than raising. An outbox with no room and a connection the
world has closed because the client's patience ran out are both facts about the
client and the wire, and this course returns a verdict about content: `sent` is
zero, `deferred` has not moved and `drained` is `False`. Only a shape mismatch
raises — a state that is not a mapping with a connection, a `data` that is not
bytes, a connection that is not this link's — and those raise `ServerError`
naming the offender. A server that never widens the outbox and never calls `write`
with an empty outbox offers the world nothing it cannot take, so the link's own
log stays quiet: `drops` is zero, and the bytes that reached the clients are
exactly the answers the result reports.
"""

from link import MAX_CHUNK

#: The turn budget a run starts from: a spent budget is an outcome this stage
#: reports, so the default only has to be big enough to finish a workload.
DEFAULT_BUDGET = 256


class ServerError(ValueError):
    """A state, a reply or a server this stage will not send through.

    It is the family for every shape `send` and `serve_backpressure` cannot
    honour: a `state` that is not a mapping, a state whose connection is not this
    link's, a state whose `pending` is not bytes or whose `offset` is not an int,
    a `data` that is not bytes, a `server` that is not the dict of the contract,
    and a `budget` that is not a whole number of turns. A verdict about what the
    client or the wire did — an outbox with no room, a connection the client
    dropped, a reply still waiting behind another — is never an exception here:
    it is `sent`, `deferred`, `drained` and `stalled` in the result.
    """


def send(link, state, data):
    """One move of one connection's reply: hand over what the outbox will take.

    `state` is the connection's state: `{"conn", "phase", "buffer", "pending",
    "offset"}` — stage 1's connection, the phase a move is taken from, the bytes
    of a request line read but never finished, the reply in flight and how far it
    has got. A `send` is a *writing* move: the state must be in the `"writing"`
    phase when it is handed over, and it goes back to `"reading"` once the whole
    reply has reached the outbox, because a connection owed nothing is a
    connection whose next move is a read. `pending` is the reply in flight and
    `offset` is how many of its bytes have reached the outbox. A state whose
    `pending` is empty starts a new reply from `data`; a state whose `pending` is
    non-empty is halfway through the reply it already holds, and `data` must then
    be exactly the bytes still owed, `pending[offset:]` — the same reply handed
    over a second time is a caller that lost the offset, and is refused naming
    what was given.

    The answer is `{"state", "sent", "deferred", "drained"}`: the state again
    (fresh, with `pending` and `offset` moved on), `sent` the bytes the outbox
    took this call, `deferred` the bytes still owed afterwards, and `drained`
    whether the whole reply has now reached the outbox. `MAX_CHUNK` is not the
    limit here — the state is — so a reply bigger than the outbox takes turns,
    and a reply bigger than `MAX_CHUNK` takes turns even when the outbox is roomy.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement send()")


def serve_backpressure(server, *, budget=DEFAULT_BUDGET):
    """A reactor whose writes are one reply at a time, and what that costs.

    `server` is the bundle every model in this course drives — `{"link",
    "clients", "requests"}` — and the answer is `{"answers", "steps", "ticks",
    "deferred", "stalled"}`. `answers` is every client's reply lines in the order
    they were written, and a reply counts when its last byte has reached the
    outbox and not when its request was read: a reply the budget left half
    written is not an answer the world carried. `deferred` names the clients
    whose reply had to be handed over in more than one turn, in accept order, and
    `stalled` the clients whose reply the whole budget never moved at all — the
    head-of-line blocking this stage exists to put a number on.

    One turn: accept everyone the listener holds, poll `ready_set` for what can
    be read, take one read move per readable connection, and write the reply at
    the head of the write queue — one outbox-full of it — if the world has room.
    A reply stays at the head until its client has taken it whole, so the replies
    behind it wait for it rather than sharing the turns; the link is stepped once
    per turn, and `steps` and `ticks` are the same count because nothing here
    moves a byte outside `Link.step()`. A spent budget is an outcome, not an
    exception: the result reports what was written and what never moved.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement serve_backpressure()")

"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 9: The Redis case study: a command loop with per-connection state.

Every stage before this one speaks the same protocol — a line in, the same line
back with a `+` in front of it — and that protocol has no memory: a request is
answered out of itself and nothing a client says changes anything for the next
one. Redis's protocol does not work that way. `SET` is remembered, `EXPIRE`
expires, `QUIT` ends the conversation, and the same connection asks its next
question against what its last answer did.

So this stage is where the state lands, and the whole subject is *which* state
lands where. The store belongs to the server: two connections that `SET` and
`GET` the same key are talking about the same key, and a client that opens a
second connection does not find a second world. The input buffer belongs to the
connection: two clients' half-read commands never mix, each connection counts its
own queries, and only one of them can have asked to quit. Getting that split
wrong is not a crash — it is a `GET` that sees a key nobody set, which is exactly
the kind of failure this course is about.

`parse` is the first layer, and its job is the *shape* of a line: a line is bytes,
it ends in a newline, and only then does it have a command and arguments at all.
`execute` is the second, and its job is the *content* of a command: an unknown
command, a wrong count of arguments and an `INCR` of something that is not a
number are verdicts it returns as error lines, because a client that types
nonsense is a fact about the client, not a broken program. `serve_commands` is
the third: the loop that reads bytes off the link, cuts them into whole lines,
executes them in the order they were written, and keeps the tail of a command it
has only half of.

DESIGN DECISION — Where does a command that arrives in two reads live? In the
connection's own buffer, and nowhere else. A read is a piece of a stream and the
line is the unit the protocol has: the buffer accumulates what the link hands
over and a command is executed exactly when its line is whole, which means a
buffer that is cleared per read loses half the command and a buffer that is
parsed per read executes a command the client has not finished writing. The
buffer travels with the connection, so a client that is slow to write and a
client that is slow to read cannot end up sharing one.

DESIGN DECISION — Which state is the server's and which is the connection's? One
store for the whole run; a buffer, a query count, a quit flag, the answers still
owed and the phase of the connection's machine all belong to the connection. The
store is created once, before the loop, and no connection ever gets a copy of it:
a store per connection would answer `GET` from a key the other client set as a
miss, which is a bug that looks exactly like a client's mistake.

DESIGN DECISION — Is an unknown command an exception or a reply? A reply — the
error line — every time. Nothing about a client's typing can make a server fail,
and a loop that raises where it could answer turns one client's typo into every
other client's outage. The same goes for a wrong count of arguments and for an
`INCR` of a value that is not an integer: they are answers, and the only
exceptions in this stage are about the *shape* of what the module itself was
handed.

DESIGN DECISION — How is an expiry recorded, and how is it checked? As a deadline
in ticks on the injected clock — `EXPIRE key n` stores `now + n` — because this
course has no wall clock and a tick is the only unit of time there is; and it is
checked on the way *out* of the store, at `GET`, `DEL`, `INCR` and `KEYS` alike.
An expired key is a miss *and* is forgotten: a key that is hidden but left in the
dict is a key `KEYS` still counts and a `DEL` still finds, which is the same bug
wearing a different hat.

DESIGN DECISION — How many commands does one read execute? Every whole line in
what was read, in the order the client wrote them, and not one command more. A
client may pipeline two requests into one write, and a loop that treats the read
as one command answers the first and silently drops the second; a loop that
treats the whole read as one line loses the argument boundaries. Each complete
line is parsed and executed on its own, and the partial tail after the last whole
line is kept.

DESIGN DECISION — When is the connection closed after `QUIT`? Only once the
`+BYE` has been drained. `QUIT` raises the connection's quit flag and answers
`+BYE`; the connection then has nothing further to read, and it is closed from
the `"closing"` phase — the same phase a connection reaches when its client has
run out of requests and has taken every answer. Closing it on the spot loses the
`+BYE` the client was promised, which the link's own drained-byte count proves.

TODO: implement `parse`, `execute` and `serve_commands` in the module below.
"""

#: The commands this server speaks. The protocol is closed: a word that is not in
#: here is answered with the error line and never with an exception, because a
#: client typing nonsense is a fact about a client, not a broken course.
COMMANDS = ("SET", "GET", "DEL", "INCR", "EXPIRE", "KEYS", "QUIT")


class ServerError(ValueError):
    """A line this stage will not parse, or a command it will not run as asked.

    It is the family for every *shape* this stage cannot honour: a line that is
    not bytes or does not end in a newline, a command token that is not ascii, a
    store that is not a dict, a state that does not carry the tick it is run at,
    a server whose link is not the world or whose clients are not `Client`s, and
    a budget that is not a whole number of turns. Every *verdict about content*
    is a reply instead: an unknown command, a wrong count of arguments, an `INCR`
    of a value that is not a number and a `GET` of a key whose deadline has
    passed are all answered with the error line, and a check reads them as bytes.
    """


def parse(line):
    """The command and its arguments, as a whole line spells them.

    The line is bytes and it ends in `"\\n"` — that is what makes it whole, and a
    line without one is the tail of a read that stopped in the middle of a
    command, which is a shape this function will not guess at: it is refused
    naming the offender, and keeping it is the loop's job, not this function's.
    The newline comes off, and so does a `"\\r"` if the client wrote one, and what
    is left is split on runs of whitespace: the first token is the command and
    the rest are its arguments, as bytes and untouched, because a value is the
    client's bytes and this stage never has an opinion about them.

    The command is upper-cased here once, so the rest of the stage compares it
    against `COMMANDS` without a second spelling of every name. A blank line
    names no command, which this function reports honestly as the empty command
    and the loop answers as one it does not know — an empty line is a client's
    mistake to hear about, not this module's to raise about.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement parse()")


def execute(store, command, args, *, conn):
    """The reply line(s) one command is answered with, against a store and a state.

    `store` is the server's and it maps a key to `(value, deadline)`: the value is
    the client's own bytes and the deadline is a tick of the injected clock or
    `None` for a key that does not expire. `conn` is this connection's state, and
    the only two things read out of it are `now` — the tick being answered at —
    and `queries`, this connection's count, which every command of every kind
    moves, an unknown one and a refused one included, because a query is a query.

    The reply is one of the protocol's shapes and nothing else: `+OK` for `SET`,
    a bulk string for `GET` and `$-1` for a miss, an integer for `DEL`, `INCR` and
    `EXPIRE`, `+BYE` for `QUIT`, and one error line for an unknown command, a
    wrong count of arguments or a value that is not a number. `KEYS` is the one
    command whose answer does not fit one key: it is a bulk string holding the
    live keys in byte order, one space between them — the smallest thing the
    protocol's own shapes can carry, and a shape a check can pin exactly.

    `SET` clears any deadline the key had (a fresh value is a fresh key), `INCR`
    keeps it (the value changed, the key did not), and `EXPIRE` arms one at
    `now + ticks` — so a deadline is always a tick on the same clock, and an
    expired key answers `:0` to a `DEL` and `:0` to an `EXPIRE`, because by then
    there is nothing there to arm. `QUIT` is the only command whose effect is on
    the connection rather than the store: it raises the state's `quit` flag, and
    closing the connection is the loop's move, taken once the `+BYE` has been
    drained, never this function's.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement execute()")


def serve_commands(server, *, budget=256):
    """The command loop: every client's lines executed against one store.

    The result is the five things this stage has to say about a run, in order:
    `answers`, every client's reply lines byte for byte in the order they were
    delivered; `steps`, the turns of this loop; `ticks`, the link's own reading at
    the end; `store`, the server's store as it was left — each key with the value
    the client set and the deadline in ticks `EXPIRE` armed, or `None`; and
    `connections`, one entry per connection the server made state for, holding its
    phase, its own `queries` count, whether it asked to quit, and the bytes of a
    command it read but never finished.

    One turn: admit everyone the listener holds, ask the world which connections
    are ready, service *those* and no others — one move each — retire every
    connection that has nothing left in either direction, and step the link once.
    Nothing moves outside `Link.step()`, so a turn with nothing ready still steps,
    and only a run with nothing readable, nothing writable and nobody left in the
    listener is over.

    The store is one dict for the whole loop, so two clients asking about the same
    key ask about the same key; the buffer, the query count and the quit flag
    belong to a connection and never move between them. `budget` is in turns: a
    budget spent with work left is an outcome, not an exception, and the run says
    what it did by reporting the store and the connections it left behind.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement serve_commands()")

"""Concurrent Servers From Scratch — stage 10: One workload, four models, and the steps it took.

Stages 1 to 5 built one machine and four ways of driving it: one client at a
time, one thread per connection, one readiness set, and one event loop with
timers. Each of them answered its own workload, and four separate answers prove
nothing. This stage runs **one** workload through all four models and reports
what each of them cost — the same clients, the same requests, the same budget,
one fresh link each — and then holds every model's own account of what it did
against the link's own log.

That is the whole claim of the course, and it is deliberately not a promise that
one model wins. `run_all` reports four step counts; `compare` says whether the
four delivered the same bytes and which one was cheapest here; `cross_check` says
whether a model's belief about its own run matches the count the link kept. A
model that answered three clients while the fourth waited, a model that dropped
the tail of a reply, and a model that stepped the link twice a turn are all
visible in those three reports and in nothing else.

DESIGN DECISION — Who owns the workload: `workload()` here, or each model? A model
that builds its own clients is a model that graded itself: the four runs are only
comparable if they are handed the same clients with the same requests, the same
budget and the same script. `workload()` is the course's own workload, and every
model is a caller of it.

DESIGN DECISION — Is the link shared by the four models, or rebuilt for each? A
shared link carries the first model's leftovers — its drained bytes, its closed
connections, its clock — into the second one's run, and the second model's step
count is then measuring the first model's work. Each model gets a fresh link
built from the same clients, and `report` is that link's own log when the run is
over.

DESIGN DECISION — Does `compare` assert, or report? It reports. Four models are
allowed to disagree — the disagreement is the finding, and a stage that raised
on the first mismatch could never say *which* client, or how far apart the two
answers were. `compare` is a body of arithmetic over the four results; the
check is what asserts.

DESIGN DECISION — Whose numbers are the tie-breaker when a model disagrees with
the world? The link's. A model's `steps`, `ticks` and `answers` are what the
model believes it did; `report` is `Link.stats()`, recomputed from the link's own
event log, and it counts what actually moved. `cross_check` compares the two and
names every key they disagree on, so a server that answered while the client
received less than the answer is caught by the world rather than by its own
bookkeeping.

DESIGN DECISION — What breaks a tie between two equally cheap models? The order
of `MODELS`. Cheapest by a dict's own iteration order would make the report
depend on how the caller happened to build the dict, and a comparison that
changes when nothing changed is not a comparison.

DESIGN DECISION — Is a step a tick? No, and that is why the report keeps both.
A step is one turn of one model's loop; a tick is the world's own unit and only
`Link.step()` produces one. Two models can spend different numbers of steps to
deliver the same bytes, which is the course's subject, and the link's tick count
is what says how much of the world each of them used up.

TODO: implement `MODELS`, `workload`, `run_all`, `compare` and `cross_check` in
the module below.
"""


class ServerError(ValueError):
    """A models list this stage will not run, or a report it will not compare.

    The family for every shape this stage cannot honour: a model name that is not
    one of the four, a `runs` that is not a dict of them, a run missing one of
    its four keys, and a result that is not one this stage produced. A verdict
    about the *workload* — a model that answered later, or cost more steps, or
    delivered different bytes — is never an exception here: it is what `compare`
    and `cross_check` are for.
    """


#: The four models, in the order ties are broken and reports are read.
MODELS = ("blocking", "threads", "reactor", "event_loop")


def workload():
    """The course's own workload: the clients every model is handed.

    `{"clients", "requests", "budget", "script"}` — the clients, the same lines
    again for a caller that wants them as data, the turn budget every model gets,
    and the script the thread model is driven by (`None` for round-robin). The
    four clients are the course's four pressures: one that answers at once, one
    with two requests, one that reads two bytes every third tick, and one
    whose request and reply are longer than a single move, so every model has to
    defer a write and none of them can be compared on a workload that never
    strains.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement workload()")


def run_all(*, models=None):
    """Every model on the same workload, each on its own link.

    `{model: {"answers", "steps", "ticks", "report"}}` — `report` is
    `Link.stats()` of the link that model ran on, so the four runs can be held
    against the world rather than against each other. Each model gets a fresh
    `Link` built from the same clients: the clients are immutable, the
    connections are not.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement run_all()")


def compare(runs):
    """The four runs side by side: the same answers, and what each one cost.

    `{"same_answers", "differences", "steps", "cheapest", "tie_breaker"}`.
    `same_answers` is whether every model delivered the same replies to every
    client as the first model in the report, `differences` names the first
    mismatch per client as `(model, client, got, want)`, `steps` is every model's
    own count, `cheapest` is the fewest steps with ties broken by `MODELS` order,
    and `tie_breaker` is `cross_check` of that cheapest run.

    Nothing is asserted and nothing is raised for a disagreement: a model that
    delivered different bytes is a finding, and the report is where a check reads
    it.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement compare()")


def cross_check(run):
    """One model's own account of its run, against the link's own log.

    `{"agree", "disagreements"}` where `disagreements` is
    `((key, ours, theirs), ...)`: `ours` is what the model's result claims (the
    bytes its answers add up to, the clients it answered, the ticks it reports)
    and `theirs` is the same key recomputed from `run["report"]`. The link keeps
    the record, so a model that believes it answered while the client received
    less is a model whose two accounts disagree, by key and by number.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement cross_check()")
files.codecraft/api.py:
"""The tiny API an authored course uses to describe its stages.

A course is a directory containing `course.py`:

    from codecraft.api import stage

    TITLE = "Build a Bloom Filter"
    DESCRIPTION = "A probabilistic set, from hashing to false-positive math."

    def check_1():
        from bloom import BloomFilter
        bf = BloomFilter(bits=64, hashes=2)
        bf.add("x")
        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
